items.title: PPU
items.text: GBA PPU notes from Sly. GBATEK is the actual reference, this is the stuff I needed to know plus gotchas

items.title: Timing
items.text:
• 1'232 cycles per line, 228 lines per frame (160 visible + 68 VBLANK) = 280'896 cycles, ~59.73 FPS
  • 240 visible pixels at 4 cycles each, but the HBLANK flag/IRQ only happens around cycle 1'006-1'008 (not 960!)
  • VCOUNT (0x04000006) current line, DISPSTAT (0x04000004) IRQs for HBLANK, VBLANK, VCOUNT match

Games change registers between lines (HBLANK IRQ or HBLANK DMA) for per-line scroll, windows, affine matrices etc. Rendering a whole frame with the final register values loses all of that. I render each visible line at HBLANK with the state at that point. Mid-line changes would need finer timing.

items.title: DISPCNT
items.text:
0-2     Mode
3       CGB mode (BIOS only)
4       Displayed page (bitmap modes)
5       OAM access during HBLANK
6       Sprite tile mapping (0=2D, 1=1D)
7       Forced blank
8-12    BG0-BG3, OBJ enable
13-15   WIN0, WIN1, OBJ window enable

mode    BG0     BG1     BG2         BG3
-----------------------------------------------
0       text    text    text        text
1       text    text    affine      -
2       -       -       affine      affine
3       -       -       240x160 16bpp, 1 page
4       -       -       240x160 8bpp (palette), 2 pages
5       -       -       160x128 16bpp, 2 pages

Bitmap modes always draw on BG2 (bit 10 must be set) and use BG2's affine parameters, so bitmaps can be rotated/scaled too.

items.title: Bitmap Modes
items.text:
• Mode 3/5: pixel is the 15-bit color directly
  • Mode 4: pixel is a palette index, 0x06000000 + 240y + x (page 1 at +0xA000)
  • Mode 4 index 0 is transparent (backdrop/sprites behind BG2 show through), same for area around a mode 5 image
  • Bitmap modes eat the first half of OBJ VRAM, sprite tiles are limited to 512-1023
  • Outside of a bitmap is always transparent, wraparound bit is ignored

items.title: 8-bit VRAM Writes
items.text:
VRAM can't be written 8 bits at a time. An strb to the BG area is duplicated into both bytes of the halfword, an strb to the OBJ area is ignored. Source

fn write_vram(&mut self, mut address: u32, width: Width, value: u32) {
    if width == Width::Byte {
        if self::vram_offset(address) >= self.obj_offset() {
            return;
        }

        address &= !1;
        self::write_memory(&mut self.vram, address + 1, width, value, self::vram_offset);
    }

    self::write_memory(&mut self.vram, address, width, value, self::vram_offset);
}

Note: OBJ area boundary depends on mode (0x10000 in tiled modes, 0x14000 in bitmap modes).

items.title: Colors
items.text:
0-4     Red
5-9     Green
10-14   Blue
15      unused

BG palette at 0x05000000, OBJ palette at 0x05000200. Entry 0 of the BG palette is the backdrop.

5 to 8 bit: (c << 3) | (c >> 2), otherwise 31 becomes 248 instead of 255.

items.title: Text Backgrounds
items.text:
BGxCNT
0-1     Priority
2-3     Tile block (16 KiB)
6       Mosaic
7       8bpp
8-12    Map block (2 KiB)
13      Wraparound (affine only)
14-15   Map size
  • 4bpp: 32-byte tiles, low nibble is the left pixel, 16 banks of 16 colors
  • 8bpp: 64-byte tiles, full 256-color palette
  • Index 0 is transparent in every bank
map entry
0-9     Tile number
10      H flip
11      V flip
12-15   Palette bank

Maps are stored in 32x32 entry blocks (2 KiB), not as one big row-major array!

size    pixels      blocks
-------------------------------------------
0       256x256     SC0
1       512x256     SC0 SC1
2       256x512     SC0 / SC1
3       512x512     SC0 SC1 / SC2 SC3

block  = (ty / 32) * (W / 256) + (tx / 32)
offset = 2 * (32 * (ty % 32) + tx % 32)
entry  = 0x06000000 + 2048 * (map_block + block) + offset

Scroll (BGxHOFS/BGxVOFS, 9 bits) wraps at the map size, e.g. HOFS 337 on a 256 wide map is 81:

let bg_x = (x + bg.hofs as usize) & (width - 1);

Flipped tiles use 7 - px / 7 - py. Palette entry is 16 * bank + index for 4bpp.

items.title: Sprites (OBJ)
items.text:
OAM at 0x07000000, 128 entries of 8 bytes, 4th halfword belongs to affine matrices.

attr0
0-7     Y
8       Affine
9       Hide (regular) / double size (affine)
10-11   Mode (normal, semi-transparent, OBJ window)
12      Mosaic
13      8bpp
14-15   Shape (square, wide, tall, -)

attr1
0-8     X
9-13    Affine matrix number (affine)
12      H flip (regular)
13      V flip (regular)
14-15   Size

attr2
0-9     Tile number
10-11   Priority
12-15   Palette bank

size    square    wide     tall
------------------------------------
0       8x8       16x8     8x16
1       16x16     32x8     8x32
2       32x32     32x16    16x32
3       64x64     64x32    32x64
  • OBJ tiles at 0x06010000 + 32n. Tile numbers count 32-byte units even for 8bpp, so 8bpp sprites should use even numbers (lowest bit ignored in 2D mapping)
  • 1D mapping: n + ty * (w / 8) + tx
  • 2D mapping: n + 32 * ty + tx
  • 8bpp: column offset doubles in both, row offset doubles in 1D only

items.title: Position Wrap
items.text:
Y is 8 bits and wraps, X is 9 bits and wraps at 512. A sprite at y = 247 with height 32 shows up at the top of the screen.

let row = (line as u8).wrapping_sub(attr.y_coordinate()) as usize;
if row >= height {
    continue;
}

Affine double size sprites have a Y wrapping exception.

items.title: Cycle Budget
items.text: 1'210 cycles per line, 954 if DISPCNT bit 5 is set. Regular sprite costs 1 cycle per pixel of width, affine costs 10 + 2 * area width. Once the budget runs out the rest of the line has no sprites, and offscreen sprites still count. Source

items.title: Layer Priority
items.text:
• Lower priority number in front, on tie lower BG number wins
  • Sprite goes in front of BGs with the same or higher priority number
  • Backdrop is behind everything (treat it as priority u8::MAX)
bg_order.sort_by_key(|&(_, priority)| priority); // stable sort keeps BG order on ties

let (mut color, bg_priority) = bg_order
    .iter()
    .find_map(|&(index, priority)| bg_lines[index][x].map(|color| (color, priority)))
    .unwrap_or((backdrop, u8::MAX));

if let Some(sprite) = sprite_line[x]
    && sprite.priority <= bg_priority
{
    color = sprite.color;
}

Blending also needs the layer right behind the top one, so track the top 2.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
WINxH   0-7 X2 (right + 1)    8-15 X1 (left)
WINxV   0-7 Y2 (bottom + 1)   8-15 Y1 (top)

WININ   0-5 WIN0 (BG0-3, OBJ, effects)    8-13 WIN1
WINOUT  0-5 outside                       8-13 OBJ window
  • Check order: WIN0 -> WIN1 -> OBJ window -> outside. First match wins
  • OBJ window = opaque pixels of sprites with mode OBJ window (not drawn themselves). Needs DISPCNT bit 12 and 15
  • No window enabled at all -> everything visible, effects allowed everywhere
  • A layer still has to be enabled in DISPCNT
if let Some(index) = (0..2).find(|&index| windows.contains(index, x, y)) {
    return Some(WindowRegion::Rectangle(index));
}

Some(if windows.obj_enabled && inside_obj_window {
    WindowRegion::Obj
} else {
    WindowRegion::Outside
})

items.title: Blending
items.text:
BLDCNT
0-5     1st target (BG0-3, OBJ, BD)
6-7     Effect (0=none, 1=alpha, 2=brighten, 3=darken)
8-13    2nd target (BG0-3, OBJ, BD)

Only the topmost and the layer right behind it matter. Alpha needs top = 1st target and below = 2nd target.

alpha:     I = min(31, (I1 * EVA + I2 * EVB) >> 4)
brighten:  I = I + (((31 - I) * EVY) >> 4)
darken:    I = I - ((I * EVY) >> 4)
  • EVA/EVB (BLDALPHA bits 0-4 / 8-12) and EVY (BLDY) treat 17-31 as 16
  • EVA + EVB can exceed 16, hence the min(31)
  • Semi-transparent sprites alpha blend with the layer behind if it's a 2nd target, regardless of BLDCNT's 1st targets and effect
  • Sprites can't blend with each other (already reduced to one sprite pixel)
  • Window effects bit must be set in the pixel's region

items.title: Mosaic
items.text:
MOSAIC
0-3     BG width - 1
4-7     BG height - 1
8-11    OBJ width - 1
12-15   OBJ height - 1

Enabled per BG (BGxCNT bit 6) and per sprite (attr0 bit 12). BG blocks are aligned to the screen and take the top-left pixel's color, i.e. round the screen position down to the block start before lookup.

items.title: Affine Backgrounds
items.text:
Differences to text BGs:

  • Always 8bpp, BGxCNT bit 7 ignored
  • Map entry is 1 byte (tile number only, no flips/banks), max 256 tiles
  • Map is square and plain row-major, no 32x32 blocks
  • Scroll registers are ignored
size    pixels        map bytes
---------------------------------
0       128x128       256
1       256x256       1'024
2       512x512       4'096
3       1024x1024     16'384

The PPU walks from the screen back into the background. Parameters are signed 8.8 fixed point (BGxPA-PD, write only), reference point BGxX/BGxY is signed 20.8 (28 bits):

px = X + PA*x + PB*y
py = Y + PC*x + PD*y
texel = (px >> 8, py >> 8)

Bigger parameter = smaller picture (it's texels per pixel, not a zoom factor). For clockwise rotation θ with magnification s:

PA =  256*cos(θ)/s     PB = 256*sin(θ)/s
PC = -256*sin(θ)/s     PD = 256*cos(θ)/s

Note: GBATEK gives PB and PC the same sign, for a normal rotation they should be negatives of each other.

To keep BG point (cx, cy) at screen point (sx, sy):

X = 256*cx - PA*sx - PB*sy
Y = 256*cy - PC*sx - PD*sy

Wraparound (BGxCNT bit 13) off -> outside of the map is transparent. Masking with all ones when off lets negative coordinates become huge usize and get caught by the same bounds check:

for dst in output.iter_mut() {
    let tx = ((x >> 8) as usize) & wrap_mask;
    let ty = ((y >> 8) as usize) & wrap_mask;
    x += matrix.pa;
    y += matrix.pc;

    if tx >= size || ty >= size {
        continue;
    }
    // ...
}

items.title: Internal Reference Points
items.text:
The above reference points are automatically copied to internal registers during each [VBLANK], specifying the origin for the first scanline. The internal registers are then incremented by dmx and dmy after each scanline. Source

  • Copy BGxX/BGxY to internal registers at VBLANK
  • Add PB/PD to the internal ones after every line
  • Writing BGxX/BGxY mid-frame updates the internal register immediately
/// Advances the internal reference points by PB/PD to the start of the next scanline.
fn step_reference_points(&mut self) {
    for i in 0..2 {
        let [_, pb, _, pd] = self.bg_matrix[i];
        self.bg_ref_internal[i][0] += pb.value();
        self.bg_ref_internal[i][1] += pd.value();
    }
}

fn reload_reference_points(&mut self) {
    self.bg_ref_internal = self.bg_ref.map(|point| point.map(ReferencePoint::value));
}

Using Y + PD*line instead of the internal register breaks anything that writes the matrix or reference point per line (mode 7 style roads).

items.title: Affine Sprites
items.text:
• Bit 9 of attr0 means double size, affine sprites can't be hidden with it
  • No flip bits, negate PA+PB (H) or PC+PD (V) instead
  • 32 matrices in OAM, matrix m: PA at 0x07000006 + 32m, PB/PC/PD each 8 bytes after
  • Transform is around the center of the sprite and the center of its on-screen area
  • Double size makes the area 2w x 2h, position is top left of that, center at (x + w, y + h)
tx = ((PA*dx + PB*dy) >> 8) + w/2
ty = ((PC*dx + PD*dy) >> 8) + h/2

dx/dy measured from the area center. Texels outside the sprite are transparent.

let (x, y) = if let Some(matrix) = matrix {
    let dx = col as i32 - (box_width / 2) as i32;
    let (tx, ty) = matrix.apply(dx, dy);
    let x = tx + (width / 2) as i32;
    let y = ty + (height / 2) as i32;

    let (Ok(x), Ok(y)) = (usize::try_from(x), usize::try_from(y)) else {
        continue;
    };

    if x >= width || y >= height {
        continue;
    }

    (x, y)
} else {
    attr.flip(col, row)
};

items.title: Vertex Skip
items.text:
An indexed position with all bits set means "skip this vertex":

format    reserved index    meaning
----------------------------------------
8-bit     0xFF              skip vertex
16-bit    0xFFFF            skip vertex

Only applies to the indexed position field! Other fields use 0xFF according to their own format (e.g. alpha 0xFF = opaque). Documented in Nintendo's US6700586B1 patent.

A skipped record doesn't occupy a corner in the strip, so 0, 1, SKIP, 2, 3 is the same quad as 0, 1, 2, 3.

The bytes still exist though! E.g. 8-bit position index + RGBA color is 5 bytes, skipped or not. The parser must consume the full record (using the current vertex format), otherwise it reads a color byte as the next position index and loses its place:

for each vertex record in the draw:
    record = consume the complete record using the current format

    if its indexed position is the reserved all ones value:
        continue

    decode the record and append its vertex

assemble the draw's triangles from the retained vertices
  • Filter skipped records before vertex decoding
  • Update the vertex count per draw, otherwise a removed record can join one draw's vertices to the next
  • Depth plane tracking for z-freeze needs to agree on which triangles exist, so it has to run on the filtered list

Code: filter_skipped_vertices

Test: vertex-skip (direct, 8-bit and 16-bit indices, all 3 should match)

items.title: z-freeze
items.text:
Lets a draw reuse the depth plane of an earlier triangle instead of its own depth. libogc: GX_SetCoPlanar(GX_ENABLE).

  • While z-freeze is off, every triangle replaces the saved plane
  • While it's on, the last plane is kept and following draws evaluate it for depth (own outline/colors/UVs, borrowed depth)
  • The reference triangle doesn't need to write color or depth to establish a plane

Plane from the 3 screen space vertices:

depth(x, y) = A*x + B*y + C

Evaluated for every pixel of the new draw, including pixels outside the original triangle, so the result can leave the 0-1 range (see below). Degenerate (line/point) triangles don't define a plane.

Dolphin's January 2015 progress report also covers this.

items.title: Plane Overflow
items.text:
Clamping the extrapolated depth to max is wrong. Hardware readbacks (GX_ALWAYS write, GX_PeekZ read), horizontal and vertical slopes give the same values:

plane depth    Wii Z24     ~
----------------------------------
0.25           0x400000    0.25
1.25           0xFFFFFF    1
4.25           0x000000    0
8.25           0x3FF7E0    0.25
12.25          0x000000    0
16.25          0x3FEFC0    0.25

Looks like a value overflowing every 8 depth units before being clamped, which fits a signed 27-bit intermediate (2^27 / 2^24 = 8, range -4 to <+4):

  • 4.25 wraps to -3.75 -> clamped to 0
  • 8.25 is a full cycle -> back to 0.25

Note: wrapping with % 1.0 gives narrow stripes instead of the broad bands seen on hardware. 27-bit is just what matches, not proven, and some exact readings still differ.

Code: plane calculation, depth shader w/ overflow

items.title: TEV Wrapping
items.text:
TEV results must be reduced to 8 bits by wrapping (keep low byte), not clamping, and not left wide. Unclamped stages keep a signed intermediate of -1024..1023.

Where the wrap happens matters:

  • A/B/C inputs read only the low byte of a register
  • D input keeps the wide (signed) value
  • Final RGB/alpha output keeps the low byte before alpha test / blending

Making every stored register 8 bits loses information too early (breaks D).

  • Input wrapping alone fixes Sunshine but not Galaxy (the eye stage creates the overflow itself)
  • Output wrapping alone fixes Galaxy and makes Sunshine almost right (off by 2)

Other bits:

  • C factor is expanded to C + (C >> 7) before multiplying so 255 represents exactly 1
  • Scaled additions round by adding 128 before >> 8

Commit 14aae5a: integer arithmetic in the regular combiners, A/B/C inputs wrapped to 8 bits, final RGB/alpha wrapped before testing. Still a mixed implementation (combiner in ints, TEV registers as normalized floats), not sure yet what the implications are.

items.title: Triangle Out of Luigi's Hand
items.text:
Thin triangle stretching from Luigi's hand across the character selection menu (look between Luigi's hand and Wario's portrait).

The affected triangle strip ended with a skip record (position index 0xFF). I fetched a position for it anyway and interpreted unrelated memory as:

[-27.166016, 15.875, 0.0]

Transforming that point and connecting it to the previous 2 corners produced the spike. A skipped record doesn't occupy a corner in the strip, so 0, 1, SKIP, 2, 3 should give the same quad as 0, 1, 2, 3.

Fix: remove skipped records before vertex decoding and update the vertex count for each draw, see Vertex Skip.

Writeup: vertex-skip: The Case of Luigi's Extra Triangle

items.title: Tops of Signs Missing
items.text:
Upper parts of the player selection signs (just below "MAIN MENU") are covered by the sky, with a straight cutoff. Geometry is all there, a later draw paints over it.

The menu does this:

  1. Draw a small shape to establish a depth plane
  2. Enable z-freeze
  3. Draw the sky over the top 112 framebuffer rows using that saved plane

Without z-freeze the sky uses its own near depth and covers the signs. That draw ends at row 112, hence the straight cutoff.

Saved plane:

Z24 = 2.650141y + 16'755'356

At pixel (100, 80) on Mario's sign:

stored depth         16'641'130
sky, own depth       0               -> 0 <= 16'641'130 passes, sky covers sign
sky, frozen plane    ~16'755'569     -> fails, sign stays visible   (y = 80.5, pixel center)
background           16'777'215      -> 16'755'569 <= 16'777'215 passes, sky fills background

Writeup: z-freeze and Mario Golf's Disappearing Menu

items.title: Flickering Floor Decals
items.text: Floor logos on the Plaza court flicker / have missing bands. Decals have nearly the same depth as the floor below them, so rounding differences make them take turns winning the depth test (Z-fighting). Sharing a depth plane via z-freeze keeps the comparison consistent.

items.title: Missing Eyes
items.text:
Mario's eyes missing on the file selection screen. The head is its own model, FileSelectDataMario, eyes use material EyeMat_v (blink animations swap its texture, see Petari).

Eye triangles are there, but every fragment fails the alpha test (blending disabled):

128 <= alpha <= 255

The open-eye texture is 64x64, every texel has alpha 255, so the texture isn't the problem.

TEV stages of the material:

  1. Stage 0 calculates an intermediate lighting value in alpha
  2. Stage 1 uses that value for color, then replaces alpha with 255
  3. Stage 2 adds a quarter of the texture alpha and a half bias, clamping disabled
alpha = 255 + 64 + 128 = 447
447 & 0xFF = 191                -> 128 <= 191 <= 255 passes

Quarter contribution: floor((255 * 64 + 128) / 256) = 64. The +128 is TEV's rounding step, not the bias (both just happen to be 128).

My old float shader did:

alpha = 1.0 + 1.0 * 0.25 + 0.5 = 1.75     -> 1.75 <= 1.0 fails

The upper bound looks redundant for an 8-bit value but isn't once a wider value reaches the comparison. Note: clamping 447 also passes (255), but that's the wrong rule. E.g. 383 wraps to 127 (fail) whereas clamping gives 255 (pass).

The decisive part of the fix is wrapping the final alpha before alpha_compare:

fn tev_wrap_alpha(value: f32) -> f32 {
    return f32(i32(round(value * 255.0)) & 255) / 255.0;
}

tev_wrap_alpha(state.regs[state.last_alpha_dest].a)

Integer arithmetic alone still leaves 447 going into the test. Adding just the helper to the old float math gives 190, the full integer calculation 191. Both pass, so the eyes coming back doesn't prove the arithmetic is right. See TEV Wrapping.

items.title: White Ocean
items.text:
Ocean on the save selection screen is completely white. Material _mat1_1 in the menu's map.bmd draws a wave layer over the water that's already there. It reads the grayscale texture HAYAwave2 twice at different scales/offsets, intensity supplies alpha.

alpha (A, B, C, D):
stage 0: (ZERO, ZERO, ZERO, TEXA)
stage 1: (ZERO, TEXA, APREV, RASA)   scale 2x, clamp off
stage 2: (ZERO, RASA, APREV, ZERO)   clamp off          <- APREV read as C

RASA is 255. Example pixel with texture samples 93 and 121:

q     = floor((2 * 121 * 93 + 128) / 256) = 88
alpha = 2 * 255 + q = 598
C     = 598 & 0xFF = 86

The C input only keeps 8 bits. Stage 2's multiply by raster alpha preserves the 86. Alpha test accepts everything, blending is on: source factor SrcAlpha, destination SrcClr with white RGB, so it's additive brightening:

new channel = min(1, b + 86/255)

Old Gecko carried the wide value into stage 2, the constant alone was 2 * 1.0 = 2.0, saturating the water to white. Clamping would also be white, only the low byte recovers the varying wave intensity.

Note: TEV expands the C factor to C + (C >> 7) before multiplying so 255 represents exactly 1. 93 is below 128 so unchanged.

Trap: wrapping only at the final output also looks almost right (88 instead of 86) because stage 2 already did math on the wide C. Needs integer math + input wrapping. See TEV Wrapping.

items.title: Huge Triangles in the Sky
items.text:
Bright triangles covering the sky during the station flyby (skinned models in general). Originally debugged in Lazuli, the screenshot reproduces it in Gecko by disabling the WPAR reset.

Skinning results get written through the gather pipe into RAM (CSkinnedModel::Calculate, allocation/cache/morphing omitted):

pipe = GXRedirectWriteGatherPipe(verts);

BuildAccumulatedTransforms(pose, layout);
BuildPoints(pipe);
// Pad the position region to a multiple of 32 bytes.
BuildNormals(pipe);

GXRestoreWriteGatherPipe();
  • CVirtualBone::BuildPoints small-count path writes X, Y, Z through the same pointer without incrementing (it's the gather port)
  • GXRedirectWriteGatherPipe flushes, waits for transfers, rewrites WPAR (same 0x0C008000), disconnects the FIFOs, saves the old PI write pointer and points PI at the workspace
  • GX later reads the arrays with base address + stride

The affected pass had 23 zero bytes pending when redirecting. Without the WPAR reset they became the start of the new workspace:

reset        offset    bytes
---------------------------------------------------
yes          0         3E A0 F9 08 3E 39 E0 1A ...
no           0-22      00 ... 00 (23 zeros)
no           23        3E A0 F9 08 3E 39 E0 1A ...

All 4'224 bytes match when shifted by 23. Data was right, stored in the wrong place. GX reads with stride 12 (3 floats), array index 12:

axis    reset          no reset
-----------------------------------------
X       0.106061       0.00956970
Y       0.183704       -3.21470e15
Z       0              8.68805e-44

Broken Y is D9 36 BC 00: negative, exponent 178 -> 2^(178-127) = 2^51. Huge before projection already, same shift also breaks the normals (lighting).

Writeup: WPAR: Why Metroid Prime's Geometry Exploded

Honorary mention: vxpm

items.title: Donald's Feet Explode
items.text:
Donald's idle animation in the laboratory starts fine, then his feet stretch and his body folds into itself. Left running, triangles cover the whole room. Same with JIT and interpreter.

Positions were already wrong in RAM (CPU skinning), so GX was fine. Worked back: vertex writes -> bone matrices -> animation keyframes -> keyframe records loaded from ARAM via DMA.

Records are 24 bytes, so most aren't 32-byte aligned. The game requests 64 bytes around the record and picks it out in the completion callback, using the original unaligned address. Record at 0x7888:

  1. DMA ignores the low 5 bits, copies from 0x7880
  2. Callback: record is 8 bytes into its block
  3. Callback skips 8 bytes and copies 24

I didn't mask the DMA registers, so DMA started at 0x7888 and the callback skipped another 8:

expected:  B + r
gecko:     (B + r) + r = B + 2r

Offsets go 16, 8, 0, 24 and repeat, so 1 in 4 records still worked. At 8/16 the extracted bytes straddle 2 records, at 24 it reads the next record entirely.

From bytes to a broken bone (example with the game's rules):

  • Time 33.54, current keyframe 25, next keyframe 0 -> t = (33.54 - 25) / (0 - 25) ≈ -0.3416 (extrapolating)
  • Slerp uses a stored angle and a sine table (4'096 entries per turn). Record says 113 units (~0.17334 rad), but the quaternions are actually arccos(0.70769) ≈ 0.78457 rad apart
  • k = trunc(0.5 + t*N) = -38, weights a = sin(151π/2048) / sin(113π/2048) ≈ 1.33102, b = sin(-38π/2048) / sin(113π/2048) ≈ -0.33778
  • |q|² = a² + b² + 2ab(q0·q1) -> |q| ≈ 1.118 instead of 1
  • Quaternion-to-matrix doesn't normalize -> bone stretches, propagates to children -> skinning

Every calculation did what it was supposed to, the bytes were just wrong.

Writeup: Goin' Quackers: Why Donald's Feet Exploded

items.title: Memory
items.text: write-gather pipe and DMA notes, mostly things that corrupt data before GX ever sees it. See Games for the bugs these caused

items.title: WPAR Reset
items.text:
Gekko's write-gather pipe combines stores into 32-byte bursts. Games write to 0xCC008000 (physical 0x0C008000, selected by WPAR) and PI writes each burst to RAM at its FIFO write pointer. Software can point PI somewhere else and disconnect GX's FIFO to build arrays in RAM.

A mtspr to WPAR invalidates the data in the buffer and sets the gather address. Source

Writing WPAR (SPR 921) discards pending bytes even if the address doesn't change. Bytes already transferred stay in RAM. Without the reset, leftover bytes end up at the start of the next buffer and shift everything.

GXRestoreWriteGatherPipe writes 31 zero bytes before restoring the FIFO: a partial burst has 1-31 useful bytes, so 31 zeros guarantee the useful tail leaves in a complete burst. The leftover padding is then discarded by the WPAR write. Order matters (pad, then reset)!

Fix (commit), needed in both interpreter and JIT runtime function:

921 => {
    sys.gekko.spr.wpar = val & !1; // bit 0 is BNE (read-only buffer status)
    sys.cp.gather_pos = 0;         // empty the pipe, no need to zero the buffer
}

Same commit also fixed redirection: PI must keep writing bursts to RAM while the CPU/GPU FIFOs are disconnected. Only the GX notification depends on the link:

write the complete burst to RAM
advance the PI write pointer

if the GPU FIFO is linked:
    update its write pointer and available byte count

retain only the incomplete tail for the next burst

items.title: ARAM DMA
items.text:
ARAM DMA works in 32-byte blocks. Main RAM address, ARAM address and length are all masked with 0x03FF_FFE0 (bit 31 of length is direction). Same masks as Dolphin.

Games may write unaligned addresses on purpose and rely on the hardware ignoring the low bits.

Fix (commit):

const ARAM_DMA_MASK: u32 = 0x03ff_ffe0;

address = written_address & ARAM_DMA_MASK;
control = written_control & (0x8000_0000 | ARAM_DMA_MASK);
  • Apply on every register write
  • Apply on savestate load too (older states may contain unmasked values)
  • Writing the lower half of the length register starts the transfer, upper half alone doesn't

items.title: Uncached byte stores
items.text:
An uncached byte store to RAM doesn't just change one byte: it overwrites both words of the aligned 8 byte block containing the address. Each word gets the full 32 bit source register rotated right by 8 * ((address & 3) + 1) bits (modulo 32).

Storing 0x12345678 to 0xD0080001 writes 0x56781234 to both 0xD0080000 and 0xD0080004. Cached byte stores only change the addressed byte.

BootMii's PPC loader relies on this when deriving its payload decryption key.

items.title: Starlet
items.text: Shoutout to Zayd :)

items.title: Memory Map
items.text:
Addresses are Starlet CPU physical addresses.

Start End (inclusive) Size Mapping 0x00000000 0x017FFFFF 24 MiB MEM1 0x10000000 0x13FFFFFF 64 MiB MEM2 with configurable Broadway access 0x0D400000 0x0D41FFFF 128 KiB window SRAM/boot ROM mapping 0xFFF00000 0xFFFDFFFF Seven 128 KiB windows Mirrors of the window at 0x0D400000 0xFFFE0000 0xFFFFFFFF 128 KiB window SRAM/boot ROM mapping

items.title: SRAM and boot ROM mapping
items.text:
SRAM consists of a 64 KiB bank A and a 32 KiB bank B. The 8 KiB boot ROM repeats every 0x2000 bytes throughout the ranges where it is mapped. Two controls decide what appears in the windows. HW_SRNPROT[SM] (0x0D800060) selects the bank arrangement and HW_BOOT0[12] (0x0D80018C) hides the boot ROM when set. Switching either control only changes the mapping. The SRAM contents stay where they are.

With the boot ROM enabled (HW_BOOT0[12] = 0):

SM Start End (inclusive) Mapping 0 0x0D400000 0x0D40FFFF SRAM A 0 0x0D410000 0x0D417FFF SRAM B 0 0xFFFE0000 0xFFFEFFFF SRAM A 0 0xFFFF0000 0xFFFFFFFF Boot ROM 1 0x0D400000 0x0D41FFFF Boot ROM 1 0xFFFE0000 0xFFFEFFFF Boot ROM 1 0xFFFF0000 0xFFFFFFFF SRAM A

With the boot ROM disabled (HW_BOOT0[12] = 1), the windows at 0x0D400000 and 0xFFFE0000 share one arrangement. Offsets are relative to the start of either window:

SM Start offset End offset (inclusive) Mapping 0 0x00000 0x0FFFF SRAM A 0 0x10000 0x17FFF SRAM B 1 0x00000 0x07FFF SRAM B 1 0x10000 0x1FFFF SRAM A

Each SRAM range maps its bank starting at byte zero. The seven windows from 0xFFF00000 through 0xFFFDFFFF mirror the window at 0x0D400000 in every configuration.

items.title: SRAM DMA addresses
items.text:
Peripheral DMA uses a fixed SRAM bank arrangement. The CPU bank swap and boot ROM mapping do not change these DMA addresses.

DMA start DMA end (inclusive) Size Mapping 0x0D400000 0x0D40FFFF 64 KiB SRAM A 0x0D410000 0x0D417FFF 32 KiB SRAM B

Each DMA range starts at byte zero of its bank. IOS converts SRAM pointers before programming the AES and SHA-1 engines.

items.title: SRAM control
items.text: Starlet physical address Width Name Purpose 0x0D800060 32 bits HW_SRNPROT SRAM access and mapping 0x0D80018C 32 bits HW_BOOT0 Boot ROM visibility

items.title: HW_SRNPROT
items.text: Bits Name Description 5 SM / IOUEN Selects the SRAM/ROM arrangement 3 U3 / AHPEN Enables Broadway access to SRAM 2 C / FLAEN Enables NAND engine access to SRAM 1 B / SHAEN Enables SHA-1 engine access to SRAM 0 A / AESEN Enables AES engine access to SRAM

items.title: HW_BOOT0
items.text:
Bits Description 12 Disables the boot ROM mappings when set. 3:0 Polled by boot1 for the value 9 during device synchronization.

While bit 12 is set, the ranges that would otherwise show the boot ROM expose SRAM according to HW_SRNPROT[SM], as listed in SRAM and boot ROM mapping.

boot1 polls bits 3:0 while it changes HW_SPARE0 (0x0D800188). Status wait before device synchronization describes the firmware sequence.

items.title: Timer alarm
items.text:
Physical address Width Access Name Purpose 0x0D800010 32 bits R HW_TIMER Timer counter 0x0D800014 32 bits W HW_ALARM Alarm deadline

Software reads the counter and writes a future counter value to HW_ALARM to request a timer interrupt. The timer interrupt uses bit 0 of HW_ARMIRQFLAG and HW_ARMIRQMASK. Writing 0x00000001 to HW_ARMIRQFLAG acknowledges it. A subsequent alarm is scheduled by writing another deadline.

The IOS alarm programming sequence clamps short delays before adding them to the counter.

items.title: ARM interrupts
items.text:
Addresses are Starlet physical addresses.

Address Width Access Name Purpose 0x0D800038 32 bits R/W HW_ARMIRQFLAG Pending ARM interrupts 0x0D80003C 32 bits R/W HW_ARMIRQMASK ARM interrupt mask

items.title: HW_ARMIRQFLAG - 0x0D800038 (32 bits, R/W)
items.text: Bit Name Description 0 Timer Pending timer alarm interrupt 1 NAND Pending NAND completion interrupt 2 AES Pending AES completion interrupt 3 SHA-1 Pending SHA-1 completion interrupt 7 SDHC Pending front SD slot interrupt 31 IPC Pending Broadway IPC interrupt

items.title: HW_ARMIRQMASK - 0x0D80003C (32 bits, R/W)
items.text:
Bit Name Description 0 Timer Mask bit for timer alarms 1 NAND Mask bit for NAND completion 2 AES Mask bit for AES completion 3 SHA-1 Mask bit for SHA-1 completion 7 SDHC Mask bit for the front SD slot 31 IPC Mask bit for Broadway IPC

The boot2 kernel's irq_handler (0xFFFF1F14) reads HW_ARMIRQFLAG, ANDs it with HW_ARMIRQMASK and handles each interrupt whose bit is set in the result. It acknowledges an interrupt by writing a value with only that interrupt's bit set to HW_ARMIRQFLAG.

items.title: OTP
items.text: OTP (one-time programmable memory) stores 128 bytes inside Hollywood. Its contents include the expected boot1 hash, the device ID and cryptographic keys. The first 20 bytes hold the boot1 hash used during boot0 verification.

items.title: OTP registers
items.text:
Addresses are physical. R means read and W means write.

Address Width Access Name Purpose 0x0D8001EC 32 bits W HW_EFUSEADDR Select an OTP word and request a read 0x0D8001F0 32 bits R HW_EFUSEDATA Read the selected OTP word

HW_EFUSEADDR fields:

Bits Name Access Description 31 Read request W Set to 1 when selecting the word to read. 4:0 Word index W Selects one of the 32 words in OTP.

HW_EFUSEDATA fields:

Bits Name Access Description 31:0 Data R The selected 32 bit OTP word.

Software writes 0x80000000 | word_index to HW_EFUSEADDR then reads HW_EFUSEDATA. Word 9 contains the device ID. Broadway software with hardware access uses these same registers through the uncached effective addresses 0xCD8001EC and 0xCD8001F0.

items.title: SEEPROM
items.text: SEEPROM is a serial EEPROM connected through GPIO. It holds console certificate data and boot version records.

items.title: Boot sequence
items.text:
1. boot0 decrypts and verifies boot1
  2. boot1 loads, decrypts and verifies boot2
  3. boot2 hands off into IOS
  4. IOS starts its kernel and service modules

BootMii runs its own Starlet firmware, MINI, in place of IOS.

Homebrew Channel runs applications through IOS. HackMii Installer prepares BootMii's SD files.

items.title: boot0
items.text: Boot0 reads boot1 from NAND into SRAM, corrects read errors, decrypts it and checks its hash against OTP before handing over execution. See the Starlet memory map for SRAM and ROM mappings.

items.title: Entry and buffers
items.text:
The reset vector at 0xFFFF0000 jumps to reset (0xFFFF0040), which sets the stack pointer and starts the loader.

ARM address Use 0xFFFF0000 Reset vector 0x0D400000-0x0D4177FF boot1 buffer, 94 KiB 0x0D417800 First spare/ECC buffer 0x0D417880 Second spare/ECC buffer 0x0D417C00 Initial stack pointer 0xFFF00000 boot1 entry through the SRAM alias

items.title: Loading and verification
items.text:
load_boot1 (0xFFFF0108) writes 7 to HW_SRNPROT (0x0D800060), which enables SRAM access for NAND, SHA-1 and AES and leaves SM clear. It then loads the AES key and IV from ROM and reads the expected hash from five OTP words, starting at index 0.

expected_hash = OTP_ReadWords(0, 5);

for (page = 0; page < 47; page++) {
    NAND_ReadPage(page, boot1 + page * 2048, spare);
    if (!ECC_CorrectPage(boot1 + page * 2048, spare))
        fatal_error(0xF1);
}

AES_CBC_Decrypt(boot1, 0x17800, rom_key, rom_iv);
actual_hash = SHA1_CalculateBlocks(boot1, 0x17800);

if (!AllZero(expected_hash) && actual_hash != expected_hash)
    fatal_error(0xF2);

jump(0xFFF00000);

items.title: Errors
items.text:
Code Meaning 0xF1 Uncorrectable ECC error 0xF2 boot1 hash mismatch

fatal_error (0xFFFF00A4) repeatedly writes the code to GPIO bits 23:16, waits, writes zero and waits again.

items.title: boot1
items.text:
boot1 is the second stage of the Starlet boot chain. boot0 loads it into SRAM, decrypts and verifies it and jumps to 0xFFF00000. boot1 then finds boot2 in NAND, checks its signature chain, decrypts and hashes it into MEM1 and jumps to it.

boot1 is a 94 KiB (0x17800 byte) image. It starts executing through the 0xFFF00000 alias of SRAM but its pointers to its own data and to some of its own functions use the 0x0D400000 alias. Both aliases refer to the same memory. The memory map shows the mappings.

items.title: Entry
items.text:
Execution starts at start (0xFFF00000) in ARM state. The entry code prepares the caches and the stack, calls the loader and then jumps to the address the loader returns. Its call to memset32 (0xFFF0005C) writes nothing because both ends of the range are 0x0D404320. Bit 12 (I) of the CP15 control register enables the instruction cache, as described in boot2 kernel entry. boot1 keeps the cache enabled only while the loader runs:

void start(void)
{
    invalidate_icache();                 // MCR p15, 0, r0, c7, c5, 0
    invalidate_dcache();                 // MCR p15, 0, r0, c7, c6, 0
    cp15_control |= 1 << 12;             // enable the instruction cache
    memset32(bss_start, bss_end, 0, 4);  // the range is empty in boot1
    sp = 0x0D40EFFC;
    void *entry = load_boot2();          // Thumb code
    cp15_control &= ~(1 << 12);          // disable the instruction cache
    goto *entry;                         // MOV PC, R1, stays in ARM state
}

items.title: Loader
items.text:
load_boot2 (0xFFF00494 in boot1b and 0xFFF004F4 in boot1d) does all the work. It writes progress code 0x11 to bits 23:16 of 0x0D8000E0, the same GPIO field that boot0 uses for its error codes. It then writes 0x47 to HW_SRNPROT (0x0D800060) if the upper four bits of the byte at 0x0D800217 are zero. Otherwise it writes 0x07.

After that, boot1 makes up to two attempts to load boot2. The first attempt searches NAND blocks 1 to 7 in ascending order. If it fails, boot1 waits for the NAND, AES and SHA-1 engines to finish and tries again, this time searching from block 7 down to block 1. If the second attempt also fails, boot1 shows the error code forever.

void *load_boot2(void)
{
    int error;

    debug_out(0x11);
    HW_SRNPROT = (read8(0x0D800217) >> 4) == 0 ? 0x47 : 0x07;

    for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 2; attempt++) {
        int first = attempt == 1 ? 1 : 7;
        int step  = attempt == 1 ? +1 : -1;

        if (attempt == 2)
            wait_until_idle(NAND, AES, SHA1);

        read_block_map(&map);
        error = load(first, step, &map, &content);
        if (error == 0) {
            write32(content + 0x0C, 1);
            debug_out(0x22);
            return content + read32(content);
        }
    }

    for (;;) {
        debug_out(error);
        delay(1000000);
        debug_out(~error);
        delay(1000000);
    }
}

debug_out(code) (0xFFF0007C) writes the low byte of code to bits 23:16 of 0x0D8000E0. The final error loop alternates the error code with its complement and calls delay (0xFFF03CD4 in boot1b and 0xFFF031AC in boot1d) after each write.

items.title: Block map
items.text:
Before each attempt, boot1 looks for a block map. It reads the last page (page 63) of every block from 1 to 7. Each of these pages can hold three copies of a 76 byte map, at offsets 0x00, 0x4C and 0x98:

Offset Size Contents 0x00 8 Magic, an 8 byte constant stored in boot1 0x08 4 Generation number, big-endian 0x0C 64 One byte per block number, 1 means skip block

A page only provides a map if at least two of its three copies are identical over all 76 bytes. boot1 uses copy 0 when its magic matches and it is identical to copy 1 or copy 2. Otherwise it uses copy 1 when its magic matches and it is identical to copy 2. If neither applies, the page provides no map. Out of all accepted copies in blocks 1 to 7, the one with the highest generation wins.

items.title: Choosing a block
items.text:
If the winning generation is greater than 1, boot1 trusts the map and skips every block whose byte is 1. If there is no usable map, it checks the blocks directly instead: it reads pages 0 and 1 of the block and skips the block if the first spare byte of either page is not 0xFF.

The first block that is not skipped, in the direction of the current attempt, holds the start of boot2. If no such block exists between 1 and 7, the attempt fails with error -4.

items.title: Reading pages
items.text:
boot1 reads a page by programming the NAND engine with these writes:

  1. 0x0D010008 = 0, 0x0D01000C = page number, 0x0D010000 = 0x9F000000.
  2. Wait until bit 31 of 0x0D010000 reads as 0.
  3. 0x0D010010 = data buffer address, 0x0D010014 = spare buffer address, 0x0D010000 = 0x8030B840.

The function returns right away. boot1 waits for bit 31 of 0x0D010000 to clear before it uses the page and corrects every header and content page with ecc_correct (0xFFF00254 in boot1b and 0xFFF00288 in boot1d).

items.title: boot2 layout
items.text:
Page 0 of the boot2 block starts with a 32 byte header. All values are big-endian:

Offset Contents 0x00 Header size, must be 0x20 0x04 Offset of the encrypted content from the start of the block 0x08 Size of the certificate chain 0x0C Size of the ticket 0x10 Size of the TMD

The content offset must not be larger than 0x20000 and must be a multiple of 64. Otherwise boot1 fails with error -5. boot1d also requires a 0xA00 byte certificate chain, a 0x2A4 byte ticket and a 0x208 byte TMD. boot1b accepts the three sizes from the header without these equality checks.

boot1 reads pages 0 up to content_offset / 0x800 of the block into MEM1 at 0x00028000. The certificate chain follows the header, the ticket follows the certificate chain and the TMD follows the ticket:

0x00028000                header (0x20 bytes)
+ 0x20                    certificate chain
+ 0x20 + certs            ticket
+ 0x20 + certs + ticket   TMD

items.title: Certificate chain
items.text:
boot1 checks five signed blobs. The checks run in this order. Offsets are relative to the start of the certificate chain:

Blob Size Expected issuer Key Certificate at 0x000 0x400 Root Root key stored in boot1 (RSA-4096) Certificate at 0x400 0x300 Root- + name of the first certificate Modulus at 0x2C8, exponent at 0x3C8 TMD TMD size Root- + first name + - + second name Modulus at 0x5C8, exponent at 0x6C8 Certificate at 0x700 0x300 Root- + name of the first certificate Modulus at 0x2C8, exponent at 0x3C8 Ticket 0x2A4 Root- + first name + - + third name Modulus at 0x8C8, exponent at 0x9C8

The certificate names are stored at 0x284, 0x584 and 0x884. Before a name is used, boot1 checks its first two characters. They must be CA, CP and XS respectively or the attempt fails with error -9.

items.title: Vulnerable verifier
items.text:
boot1b checks each blob with verify_signed (0xFFF003A4). The function copies the blob to MEM1 at 0x000AC000 with mem_copy (0xFFF03ABC) and compares its 64 byte issuer field with the expected issuer string using memcmp (0xFFF039D4). It then hashes everything from the issuer field to the end of the blob with SHA-1 and checks an RSA signature over that hash:

int verify_signed(const u8 *blob, const char *issuer, const u8 *modulus,
                  const u8 *exponent, int kind, u32 size)
{
    u8 *copy = (u8 *)0x000AC000;
    u32 body    = kind == 1 ? 0x240 : 0x140;  // kind 1: RSA-4096, kinds 2-4: RSA-2048
    u32 key_len = kind == 1 ? 0x200 : 0x100;

    mem_copy(copy, blob, size);
    if (memcmp(copy + body, issuer, 64) != 0)
        return -8;

    u8 hash[20] = SHA1(copy + body, size - body);
    u8 m[key_len] = RSA_Public(copy + 4, modulus, exponent);  // m = sig^e mod n, big-endian
    if (strncmp(m + key_len - 20, hash, 20) != 0)
        return -8;

    return 0;
}

The signature starts at offset 4 of the blob. The 32 bit value at offset 0 is not looked at. The public exponent is stored as 4 big-endian bytes. boot1 drops any trailing zero bytes before using it.

The boot1b check has two flaws:

  1. Only the last 20 bytes of m are compared with the hash. The padding in front of them is ignored.
  2. The comparison uses strncmp (0xFFF03C74), which stops at the first position where both strings contain a zero byte. If the first byte of the hash is 0x00 and the matching byte of m is also 0x00, the check passes no matter what the remaining 19 bytes are.

items.title: Fixed verifier
items.text:
boot1d checks each blob with verify_signed (0xFFF003D8). The blob must start from 0x00028000 through 0x00048000 and its size must not exceed 0x3FFF. The function copies it to 0x000AC000 with mem_copy (0xFFF028CC) then checks the issuer with memcmp (0xFFF02ED0) and hashes the signed body. A failed issuer or RSA check returns error -8.

rsa_verify (0xFFF034D8) checks the complete EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 encoded message. It requires the initial 0x00 0x01, every 0xFF padding byte, the 0x00 separator, the SHA-1 DigestInfo encoding and all 20 digest bytes. The accepted message is:

00 01 FF ... FF 00 30 21 30 09 06 05 2B 0E 03 02 1A 05 00 04 14 <20 byte SHA-1>

The first root certificate uses a 512 byte encoded message. The remaining four blobs use 256 byte encoded messages. A zero signature decodes to zero and fails the initial bytes, padding and digest checks.

items.title: Decryption and hashing
items.text:
Once all signatures pass, boot1 decrypts the content key, checks the TMD and loads the content:

  1. It decrypts the 16 bytes at offset 0x1BF of the ticket with AES-128-CBC. The key is a constant stored in boot1. The IV is the 8 bytes at offset 0x18C of the TMD followed by 8 zero bytes. This decryption happens in place at MEM1 0x000B0000 and boot1 clears that buffer afterwards.
  2. It checks that the two big-endian words at offsets 0x18C and 0x190 of the TMD are both 1. Otherwise the attempt fails with error -11.
  3. It checks that the byte at offset 0x18B of the TMD is at least version byte 0 of the SEEPROM version record. If it is smaller or if no valid record can be read, the attempt fails with error -10.
  4. It takes the content size from the word at offset 0x1F0 of the TMD and the expected SHA-1 hash from offset 0x1F4 and builds the content IV from the 2 bytes at offset 0x1E8 followed by 14 zero bytes.

The content then streams from NAND into MEM1. The page that contains the content offset is loaded to 0x00028000, so the content itself starts at 0x00028000 + (content_offset & 0x7FF). Later pages follow in order. When boot1 reaches the end of a block, it continues with the next block in the direction of the current attempt, skipping blocks the same way as before. The content size is rounded up to a multiple of 16 bytes and the spare buffers are placed right behind the content. If round_up(0x00028800 + (content_offset & 0x7FF) + padded_size, 128) + 256 is larger than 0x7FFFF or if boot1 runs out of blocks, the attempt fails with error -6.

The pages move through a three-stage pipeline. While the NAND engine reads one page, the previous page is corrected and decrypted in place and the page before that is hashed. All of the content is decrypted as one AES-128-CBC stream with the decrypted content key. The first AES command written to 0x0D020000 is 0x98000000 | (length / 16 - 1) and every following one is 0x98001000 | (length / 16 - 1). The SHA-1 hash covers exactly the content size rather than the padding to 16 bytes and uses standard SHA-1 padding. If the hash does not match the TMD, the attempt fails with error -7.

items.title: SHA-1
items.text: The SHA-1 engine only processes whole 64 byte blocks, so boot1 adds the padding itself. To finish a hash, it builds the last one or two blocks in MEM1 at 0x000A8000: the leftover bytes, a 0x80 byte, zeros and the message length in bits. Only the low 32 bits of the length are written. The upper 32 bits are always zero.

items.title: ECC correction
items.text:
ecc_correct checks a 2048 byte page in four 512 byte chunks. For each chunk it compares the ECC word stored in the spare area at 0x30 + 4 * i with the word the NAND engine calculated at 0x40 + 4 * i:

int ecc_correct(u8 *data, u8 *spare)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
        u32 stored   = read32(spare + 0x30 + 4 * i);
        u32 computed = read32(spare + 0x40 + 4 * i);
        if (stored == computed)
            continue;

        u32 diff = bswap32(stored) ^ bswap32(computed);
        if ((diff & (diff - 1)) == 0)
            continue;               // only one bit differs: the error is in the ECC itself

        if (((diff & 0xFFF) ^ (diff >> 16)) != 0xFFF)
            return -1;              // the data cannot be corrected

        u32 byte = (diff >> 19) & 0x1FF;
        u32 bit  = (diff >> 8) & 7;
        data[i * 512 + byte] ^= 1 << bit;
    }
    return 0;
}

items.title: Engine handshake
items.text:
Before every AES or SHA-1 command and after every NAND read or AES command, boot1 runs the ahb_mem_flush (0xFFF01744) handshake. It writes a mask to the 16 bit register at 0x0D8B4228 and then reads the 16 bit register at 0x0D8B422A until it returns the same mask, calling udelay(1) (0xFFF024DC) between reads. When the register matches or after 1,000,000 failed reads, boot1 writes 0 back to 0x0D8B4228.

When Mask Before a SHA-1 or AES command 1 After a NAND read 8 After an AES command 2

If the register never matches, boot1 prints ERROR: ahbMemFlush(0x%x) did not ack! and carries on. The message goes out through ARM semihosting, never had to deal with this so take it with a grain of salt pls: a Thumb SVC 0xAB with R0 = 4 (SYS_WRITE0) and R1 pointing at the text. boot1 sends the text in pieces of up to 15 characters.

items.title: Synchronization after a register read
items.text:
Each acknowledgement poll goes through memreg_read_sync(0x22A) (0xFFF01724). This helper reads the 16 bit register at 0x0D8B422A, calls ahb_sync_dev(0) (0xFFF014EC) and then returns the value it read before that call.

ahb_sync_dev(0) works on bit 15 of the 32 bit register at 0x0D8B0008.

Register Bit Use by boot1 0x0D8B0008 15 Skips the device 0 sequence when set. Otherwise pulsed as shown below.

If bit 15 already reads as one, the call returns without writing the register. Otherwise boot1 makes four 32 bit writes based on the value it read: one with bit 15 clear, followed by three with bit 15 set. The other bits keep their values from that original read.

items.title: Status wait before device synchronization
items.text:
Before it submits SHA-1 input, boot1 calls ahb_sync(5) (0xFFF01800), which runs ahb_sync_dev(5) and then ahb_sync_dev(0). Devices 2 through 10 share one branch of ahb_sync_dev. Each selects mask 1 << (device - 2) in the 32 bit register at 0x0D8B0008, so device 5 selects bit 3 (0x00000008). If the selected bit already reads as one, the call returns immediately.

Otherwise boot1 polls the low four bits of HW_BOOT0 (0x0D80018C) while it changes HW_SPARE0 (0x0D800188) and several other control registers. It reads 0x0D8B0008 through mc_read (0xFFF014A0):

Register Bits Use by boot1 HW_SPARE0 (0x0D800188) 25 Set before the second wait. Cleared during cleanup. HW_SPARE0 (0x0D800188) 16 Set on every pass of the first wait while HW_BOOT0[3:0] is 9. Cleared afterwards. HW_BOOT0 3:0 Polled until it leaves 9, then polled again after setup until it reaches 9. 0x0D800124 10:6 Set to 10 during setup and to 3 during cleanup. Bit 10 is clear in both values. 0x0D800134 10 Set before the second wait. Cleared during cleanup. 0x0D800100 through 0x0D800120, every 4 bytes 10 Set in each register after the second wait. Cleared during cleanup. 0x0D8B0008 8:0 Devices 2 through 10 select bits 0 through 8. A set bit skips the sequence. 0x0D800214 7:4 Tested by mc_read to decide whether it sets and later restores 0x0D800130. 0x0D800130 10 Set by mc_read before four discarded reads of 0x0D800138 when that path is taken.

All accesses in the sequence are 32 bits at Starlet physical addresses. set32 and clear32 each read the register fresh and write it back with only the given bits changed. replace32 reads the register, clears the mask and inserts the given value:

void ahb_sync_dev(u32 device)  // devices 2 through 10
{
    u32 mask = 1u << (device - 2);
    if ((mc_read(8) & mask) != 0)
        return;

    while ((read32(HW_BOOT0) & 0xF) == 9)
        set32(HW_SPARE0, 0x00010000);

    clear32(HW_SPARE0, 0x00010000);
    set32(HW_SPARE0, 0x02000000);
    replace32(0x0D800124, 0x000007C0, 0x00000280);
    set32(0x0D800134, 0x00000400);

    while ((read32(HW_BOOT0) & 0xF) != 9) {}

    for (u32 address = 0x0D800100; address <= 0x0D800120; address += 4)
        set32(address, 0x00000400);

    write32(0x0D8B0008, mc_read(8) & ~mask);
    write32(0x0D8B0008, mc_read(8) | mask);

    clear32(0x0D800134, 0x00000400);
    for (u32 address = 0x0D800100; address <= 0x0D800120; address += 4)
        clear32(address, 0x00000400);
    clear32(HW_SPARE0, 0x02000000);
    replace32(0x0D800124, 0x000007C0, 0x000000C0);
}

The first loop waits for HW_BOOT0[3:0] to leave 9 and the second waits for it to reach 9. Both compare against 9 for every device in this branch. Neither loop has a timeout or calls udelay. boot1 never writes HW_BOOT0 during the sequence. The two writes to 0x0D8B0008 happen only after the second wait. The SHA-1 command is issued after ahb_sync returns.

Both writes to 0x0D800124 clear bit 10. The setup write puts 10 into bits 9:6 and the cleanup write puts 3 there. Cleanup clears the bits that setup set instead of restoring their entry values. It returns without polling HW_BOOT0 again.

mc_read(offset) reads the word at 0x0D8B0000 | offset. If bits 7:4 of 0x0D800214 read as zero on entry, it first saves 0x0D800130, sets bit 10 there and reads 0x0D800138 four times, discarding the values. After reading the requested word, it reads 0x0D800214 twice. If bits 7:4 of the second read are zero, it writes the saved value back to 0x0D800130. When the entry test found a nonzero field, nothing was saved and this restore writes zero.

items.title: udelay
items.text:
udelay(n) busy-waits on the counter at 0x0D800010. It converts n to a number of counter ticks by adding shifted copies of n:

u32 ticks = scale
    ? n + (n >> 1) + (n >> 2) + (n >> 3) + (n >> 6) + (n >> 8) + (n >> 9) + (n >> 10) + (n >> 12)
    : n + (n >> 2) + (n >> 6);
if (ticks < 2)
    ticks = 2;

scale (0x0D404314) is a word in boot1's data that holds 1. The wait handles the counter wrapping around.

items.title: SEEPROM
items.text: boot1 accesses SEEPROM through GPIO. It calls delay(125) before and after raising the clock for each bit.

items.title: SEEPROM version record
items.text:
The SEEPROM holds two copies of a 10 byte version record, at byte offsets 0x48 and 0x52. All values are big-endian:

Offset Size Contents 0x00 1 Version byte 0, the lowest allowed value for TMD byte 0x18B 0x04 4 Counter 0x08 2 Checksum: the sum of the four 16 bit words at 0x00-0x07, truncated to 16 bits

A copy is valid when its checksum matches. Among the valid copies, boot1 uses the one with the highest counter. If neither copy is valid, the version check fails.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
When both attempts fail, the GPIO debug field alternates between the low byte of the error code and its complement.

Code Shown Meaning -1 0xFF / 0x00 A page has an error that ECC cannot correct -4 0xFC / 0x03 No usable block between 1 and 7 -5 0xFB / 0x04 The header is invalid -6 0xFA / 0x05 The content is too large or boot1 ran out of blocks -7 0xF9 / 0x06 The content hash does not match the TMD -8 0xF8 / 0x07 An issuer does not match or a signature check failed -9 0xF7 / 0x08 A certificate name does not start with CA, CP or XS -10 0xF6 / 0x09 The TMD version is too old or the SEEPROM record is invalid -11 0xF5 / 0x0A The TMD title ID is not 00000001-00000001

items.title: boot2
items.text: boot1 loads boot2 into MEM1 and jumps to its ELF loader.

items.title: ELF loading
items.text:
The ELF loader runs before the boot2 kernel. It first reads HW_SRNPROT (0x0D800060) and sets bit 5 (SM) if it is clear. While the boot ROM is enabled, this arrangement places SRAM bank A at 0xFFFF0000 (see SRAM and boot ROM mapping).

The loader then walks the ELF program headers. For each header of type PT_LOAD (1), it copies p_filesz bytes from ELF base + p_offset to the physical address p_paddr. The kernel segments are among them and load at 0xFFFF0000 and above.

items.title: Kernel entry
items.text:
The kernel starts at 0xFFFF0000 with a jump to init_kernel (0xFFFF0054). This routine invalidates the instruction and data caches. It then sets two bits in the CP15 control register c1:

Bit Name Description 12 I Enables the instruction cache. 1 A Enables alignment checking for data accesses.

Alignment checking applies even while the memory management unit (MMU) is disabled. Word accesses must be aligned to 4 bytes and halfword accesses to 2 bytes. A misaligned access raises a Data Abort. Byte accesses never fault.

Next, init_kernel uses fill_word_range (0xFFFF0040) to clear the kernel's uninitialized data, which lies in two SRAM ranges. The first range is in bank A at 0xFFFF0000 and above. Setting HW_BOOT0[12] (0x0D80018C) afterwards disables the boot ROM and exposes bank B at 0xFFFE0000 for the second range:

fill_word_range(0xFFFF9C80, 0xFFFFEB40, 0, 4);
HW_BOOT0 = HW_BOOT0 | (1u << 12);
fill_word_range(0xFFFE0000, 0xFFFE7CC0, 0, 4);

fill_word_range(start, end, value, stride) writes the 32 bit value to start, start + stride and so on, as long as the address is below end.

Finally, init_kernel sets the stack pointer of each privileged mode and jumps to kernel_main (0xFFFF0114) in Thumb state.

items.title: MMU initialization
items.text:
boot2's kernel enables the MMU in init_mmu (0xFFFF5184). It first disables the MMU and the data cache and then builds a 16 KiB first-level translation table at physical 0x13850000. All initial mappings are identity mappings. Wherever the address is 1 MiB aligned and at least 1 MiB of the range remains, init_mmu maps a 1 MiB section. Elsewhere it maps 4 KiB small pages through coarse second-level tables.

Descriptor Type (bits 1:0) Base address bits Section 2 31:20 Coarse table 1 31:10 Small page 2 31:12

A first-level descriptor with type 0 raises a section translation fault. The processor writes status 5 to the data fault status register and writes the faulting virtual address to the fault address register before taking a Data Abort.

Once the tables are built, init_mmu clears the data fault status, instruction fault status and fault address registers. It writes 0x13850000 to the translation table base register (CP15 c2) and calls enable_mmu (0xFFFF237C), which performs these steps in order:

  1. Writes 0x55555555 to the domain access control register (CP15 c3), which makes all 16 domains clients.
  2. Drains the write buffer.
  3. Invalidates the instruction and data TLBs.
  4. Reads the CP15 control register c1, sets bits 0 and 2 and writes it back.
Bit Name Effect of the final control write 2 C Enables the data cache 0 M Enables the MMU

items.title: Kernel services
items.text: The IOS page describes kernel services and module interfaces. NAND initialization describes how boot2 submits NAND commands and handles their completion.

items.title: BootMii
items.text: BootMii consists of the MINI firmware on Starlet and a graphical interface on Broadway. HackMii Installer prepares their SD files.

items.title: USB Gecko detection
items.text:
MINI's gecko_init (0xFFFF1728) clears the EXI channel status registers at 0x0D806800, 0x0D806814 and 0x0D806828 then calls gecko_isalive (0xFFFF165C). The detection routine probes EXI channel 1 with 32 bit accesses:

Physical address Name Use 0x0D806814 EXI1_CSR Writes 0xD0 to select the device and zero to deselect it 0x0D806820 EXI1_CR Starts a transfer and polls for completion 0x0D806824 EXI1_DATA Supplies the command and reads the response

Each transfer starts with a write to EXI1_CR. The routine then waits for the transfer start bit to clear before it starts the next transfer or reads the response:

Bit Name Firmware use 0 Transfer start Polled until clear

The routine first writes zero to EXI1_DATA and 0x19 to EXI1_CR. Once that transfer completes it writes 0x39 and waits again. A nonzero response rejects the device. After a zero response it sends 0x90000000 with control value 0x19 and requires 0x0470 in the upper 16 bits of the response.

None of these polling loops has a timeout. If the device is rejected, the routine returns without enabling the USB Gecko console.

items.title: SD card startup
items.text:
MINI's sdhc_init (0xFFFF3F24) enables ARM interrupt 7 and initializes the front SD slot at physical address 0x0D070000. sdhc_host_found (0xFFFF3E3C) resets the host and reads its capabilities. The base clock must be nonzero and between 10 MHz and 63 MHz. DMA is enabled when the host reports SDMA support.

Register offset Bits Field Firmware use 0x24 16 Card inserted Checked for an inserted card before discovery 0x40 13:8 Base clock Read in MHz and converted to kHz 0x40 22 SDMA support Enables DMA transfers when set

sdhc_start_command (0xFFFF3AF4) waits until the command path is free before writing the argument and the transfer command. For a data transfer it also programs the DMA address and the block size and count. sdhc_exec_command (0xFFFF3CC4) waits for the command to complete and copies the response before it handles data completion.

sdhc_transfer_data (0xFFFF3A38) waits for either transfer complete or a DMA boundary interrupt. At a DMA boundary it reads the DMA address register at offset 0x00 and writes the same value back to resume the transfer. Transfer complete ends the wait.

Normal interrupt bit Meaning Firmware action 0 Command complete Reads the command response 1 Transfer complete Finishes the data transfer 3 DMA boundary Writes the current DMA address back

items.title: Card capacity
items.text:
MINI's sdmmc_needs_discover (0xFFFF67D0) reads the card-specific data (CSD) with CMD9. For a standard-capacity card it uses these fields:

CSD bits Field Meaning 83:80 READ_BL_LEN Base-2 logarithm of the maximum read block length in bytes 73:62 C_SIZE Device size factor minus one 49:47 C_SIZE_MULT Base-2 capacity multiplier exponent minus two

The routine computes the capacity with unsigned 32 bit arithmetic:

capacity_bytes = (C_SIZE + 1) * (4 << C_SIZE_MULT) * (1 << READ_BL_LEN)
sector_count = capacity_bytes >> 9

It then selects the card and sends CMD16 with argument 512. The transfer block length is therefore 512 bytes even when READ_BL_LEN describes a larger maximum block. For example, C_SIZE = 4095, C_SIZE_MULT = 7 and READ_BL_LEN = 10 describe 2 GiB and produce 4194304 sectors.

items.title: Idle wait
items.text:
MINI's ipc_process_slow (0xFFFF05F8) processes queued IPC requests. Once the queue is empty it saves the interrupt mask and masks IRQ and FIQ through irq_kill (0xFFFF49A8). It checks the queue once more and then executes wait-for-interrupt. After waking up it restores the saved mask through irq_restore (0xFFFF49BC).

Checking the queue again with interrupts masked closes the window in which an interrupt could fill the queue between the empty check and the wait. For this to work, a pending interrupt has to wake the CPU from the wait even while IRQ and FIQ are masked. The exception itself is taken once the mask is restored.

items.title: PPC payload unpacking
items.text:
The PPC loader's unpack_and_boot (0x9001040C) derives an AES key from its own code and a 256 byte scratch area at 0xD0080000. It fills the scratch area with uncached byte stores and mixes the resulting bytes into the key, so the derived key depends on the uncached byte store behavior.

The loader then decrypts its compressed payload in place and decompresses the GUI ELF to 0x90100000. It repeats the code check before loading the ELF and again before entering it. If decompression fails, the loader loops forever toggling the disc slot light.

items.title: Broadway register access
items.text:
The GUI's ipc_init (0x8000A9E4) reads the pointer to MINI's IPC information header from 0xD3FFFFFC. It only uses the shared queues if the header contains the three byte magic IPC and protocol version 1. The GUI reaches the IPC registers through the 0xCD800000 window:

Broadway address Physical address Register 0xCD800000 0x0D800000 PPCMSG 0xCD800004 0x0D800004 PPCCTRL 0xCD800008 0x0D800008 ARMMSG 0xCD800030 0x0D800030 HW_PPCIRQFLAG 0xCD800034 0x0D800034 HW_PPCIRQMASK

ipc_post (0x8000A6E8) fills in a 32 byte request in the input queue and flushes it from the data cache. It advances the input tail, wrapping at the queue capacity, writes the new tail to the low 16 bits of PPCMSG and writes 1 to PPCCTRL to notify MINI.

PPCMSG bits Meaning in MINI's queue protocol 31:16 Output queue head 15:0 Input queue tail

MINI passes queue indices through the mailbox registers, unlike IOS, which passes request and reply pointers.

The GUI's gecko_init (0x800090E8) probes EXI channel 1 through 0xCD806814, 0xCD806820 and 0xCD806824. These are the same channel registers that MINI's detection routine uses.

items.title: Launching installed titles
items.text:
The GUI's launch_menu_title (0x8000E46C) picks the title ID for the Wii or Homebrew Channel icon. boot_title (0x8000B2C8) then sends MINI request 0x00050000 with the high and low words of the title ID as its two arguments.

Menu item Title ID Wii 00000001-00000002 Homebrew Channel 00010001-4C554C5A

MINI's boot2_ipc (0xFFFF5CA8) replies with the selected boot2 copy and waits for Broadway to consume the reply before it prepares the launch. If boot2 initialization failed, it replies with -1 instead.

boot2_run (0xFFFF5B40) decrypts boot2 to 0x11000000. For any title other than the System Menu it replaces boot2's default title ID and requires exactly one matching patch location. It writes 0x42 to the payload header's argument at 0x1100000C and returns the entry address, which is the payload base plus the header size. With a 16 byte header the entry is 0x11000010.

MINI shuts down its IPC service, interrupts and memory translation before entering boot2. From there boot2 launches IOS and the title. Selecting either icon therefore exits MINI instead of running the title alongside it.

items.title: HackMii Installer
items.text: HackMii Installer 1.2 runs on Broadway and uses IOS services. It prepares the SD files used by BootMii. Function addresses on this page are Broadway effective addresses.

items.title: SD files
items.text:
Preparing the SD card writes these files:

Path Contents sd:/bootmii/armboot.bin MINI firmware for Starlet sd:/bootmii/ppcboot.elf BootMii's Broadway payload sd:/bootmii/bootmii.ini BootMii configuration

items.title: Mounting the SD card
items.text:
mount_sd (0x80020F8C) calls mount_fat (0x80024010) then changes the current directory to sd:/.

Result Meaning -1 FAT mounting failed. -2 FAT mounting succeeded but changing directory failed.

The FAT mount routine initializes the SD interface and checks whether a card is inserted before reading a volume. It accepts a FAT boot sector directly at sector zero, so an MBR is not required for that layout.

items.title: Log flushing across IOS reload
items.text:
prepare_installer_ios (0x80010770) flushes the log before and after reloading IOS. flush_log (0x800224B4) mounts the SD card then calls write_sd_file (0x80021058). If the file write fails, it returns -2 without calling unmount_sd (0x80020F50). The SD initialization flag and handle remain set on this error path.

After the IOS reload, that retained initialization state can skip opening a fresh SD handle. get_sd_status (0x80043EF4) then queries the stale handle. sd_is_inserted (0x80043F48) tests bit 0 of the returned value:

Bit Use 0 A set bit reports an inserted card. A clear bit reports no card.

An IOS result of -4 has bit 0 clear. The insertion check therefore fails and the next mount returns -1 before reading sectors. IOS SD write protection can reject the earlier log write even when reads from the card succeed.

items.title: Homebrew Channel
items.text: Homebrew Channel runs on Broadway and uses IOS services. BootMii launches its installed title through boot2 and IOS.

items.title: Startup hardware checks
items.text:
In Homebrew Channel 1.1.2, check_ios_access (0x81344698) compares IOS results with direct hardware reads. Function addresses on this page are Broadway effective addresses.

get_device_id (0x8138B044) requests the device ID through ES ioctlv 7. The startup routine then performs these accesses:

Broadway effective address Physical address Access Check 0xCD800064 0x0D800064 32 bit read Requires HW_AHBPROT to equal 0xFFFFFFFF. 0xCD8001EC 0x0D8001EC 32 bit write Writes 0x80000009 to select OTP word 9. 0xCD8001F0 0x0D8001F0 32 bit read Requires the OTP device ID to match the ES result. 0xCD410008 0x0D410008 32 bit read Checks the IOS exception-vector instruction. 0xCD410028 0x0D410028 32 bit read Reads the exception handler address.

The routine also checks the instruction at the handler address through the SRAM window. These reads access the IOS code held in SRAM. The device-ID comparison uses the OTP command and data registers.

items.title: SD applications
items.text:
An application directory under sd:/apps/ can contain boot.elf and meta.xml. The browser uses the metadata for the application's name, author, version and descriptions. Selecting the application opens its details dialog. Selecting Load executes the application.

The Wii Remote D-pad and A button navigate the browser and its dialogs. Launching HackMii Installer follows the same application-loading path.

items.title: NAND
items.text: The storage layout and page operations assume a HY27UF084G2M NAND chip.

items.title: Makeup
items.text:
The NAND is made up of a list of clusters. Each cluster is made of 64 pages, and each page is made up of 2K (0x800) bytes, plus an additional spare 64 bytes. The spare can be used for various purposes, for example being able to tell if a block is bad, or detecting corruption using ECC. The first byte of the spare is 0xFF iff the block is valid. The last 16 bytes of spare seem to contain the software-calculated ECC for the page.

Warning

On startup, boot2 will do an initial scan of all blocks. For any blocks it detects are bad (by reading the first byte of spare), it will clear out the cluster.

items.title: Reads
items.text:
The NAND seems to have an internal buffer of size 0x840 - the exact length of a page plus its spare. Reads seem to follow two phases. First, read the data from the actual NAND storage into the internal buffer. Then, read the buffer out of the device, into the Starlet.

The Starlet will usually initiate three commands in quick succession when it wants to perform a read:

  1. 0x00 (Seems to move the requested page into the internal buffer)
  2. 0x01 (ditto, but for the spare bytes?)
  3. 0x30 (Read confirm - actually do the read)

This is all well and good. It would be, if the NAND interface wasn't written by a fucking dumbass. There's two buffers provided by the Starlet to the NAND interface - NAND_DATABUF and NAND_ECCBUF.

Well, actually THREE buffers, because there's a hidden third buffer at NAND_ECCBUF ^ 0x40. The three buffers operate in ways that defy logic:

  1. The first 0x800 bytes that are read, whatever they may be, goes in NAND_DATABUF.
  2. The next 0x40 bytes, if they are read, must be the spare. And so they go in NAND_ECCBUF. Notably, there is an issue in nomenclature and this should probably be called NAND_SPAREBUF but I digress.
  3. And finally, 0x10 bytes of hardware-calculated ECC are written to NAND_ECCBUF ^ 0x40.

Tip

If you happen to be writing an emulator... just write the last 0x10 bytes of the spare out to NAND_ECCBUF ^ 0x40. Saves you from having to do an ECC calculation yourself :) I honestly just discovered that I can create these cool Tip / Warning blocks and am getting a kick out of it.

items.title: Cluster Erases
items.text:
There are two commands sent to erase stuff:

  1. 0x60 (program in the cluster you want to erase)
  2. 0xD0 (confirm, do the erase)

Boot2's NAND_EraseCluster function looks roughly like this: 

int NAND_EraseCluster(uint cluster) {
  int result;
  astruct_2 *iVar1;

  if (cluster < (uint)(1 << (_MAX_CLUSTERS - 14 & 0xff))) {
    // possibly NAND_Initialized?
    if (_DAT_20009000 == 0) {
      nand_status = -10;
    } else {
      _NAND_CONFIG = _NAND_CONFIG & 0x7fffffff;

      Nand_ProgramRowCol(-1, cluster << (0xeU - _DAT_2004f1a4 & 0xff));

      result = Nand_SendCommand(0x60, a1_through_5_requested_set_erase & 0x1c,0,0);
      if (result != 0) {
        // enable interrupts
        result = Nand_SendCommand(0xD0,0,0x40008000,0);
        if (result != 0) {
            result = Nand_ReadStatus();
        }
      }
    }
  } else {
    result = -4;
  }

  _NAND_CONFIG = _NAND_CONFIG | 0x80000000;

  // who knows, and honestly who cares
  FUN_13a10048(cluster,0,nand_status);

  return result;
}

items.title: Filesystem page programming
items.text:
The filesystem programs a page in three transfers. It sets the row address to the target page and uses the column address to select the data or spare area.

Step Command Column Transfer length Control value Operation 1 0x80 0x000 0x800 bytes 0xDF805800 Transfers page data from NAND_DATABUF. 2 0x85 0x800 0x40 bytes 0xC3854040 Transfers spare data from NAND_DATABUF after changing that buffer address. 3 0x10 Unchanged 0 bytes 0xC0108000 Confirms programming.

The filesystem waits for completion between commands and reads status after the confirm command. The spare transfer supplies the page metadata separately from the 0x800 byte data transfer.

items.title: ReadStatus
items.text: Pretty simple. For NAND status, it seems like returning 0xE0 is good enough for Boot2 to think that your commands have completed successfully.

items.title: NAND completion events
items.text:
During boot2 startup, the filesystem process (process 2) registers event 1 on a message queue with message value 1. It then writes 0xC0FF8000 to the NAND control register (0x0D010000) to reset the chip and waits for the completion message.

The kernel's irq_handler (0xFFFF1F14) handles NAND completion when bit 1 is set in both HW_ARMIRQFLAG and HW_ARMIRQMASK. It writes 0x7FFFFFFF to the NAND control register and 0x00000002 to HW_ARMIRQFLAG (0x0D800038). It then calls deliver_event (0xFFFF1E34) with event 1.

deliver_event appends the event's registered message to its queue. If a thread is waiting on that queue, the thread moves to the ready queue with a successful wait result. Events without a registered queue and events whose queue is full are dropped. Once resumed, the filesystem thread receives the message and continues NAND initialization.

items.title: NAND command results
items.text:
The filesystem process submits NAND commands with send_nand_command (0x20000110, process 2 virtual address). A completion message alone does not mean that the command succeeded, so the routine also reads the NAND control register (0x0D010000) and checks its error bit:

Bit Field Firmware use 31 Busy Polls until clear when waiting without an interrupt 29 Error Returns -1 if set after completion

For an interrupt-driven command, the result is -9 if the receive fails or the message value is not 1. After this failure or a controller error, the routine writes 0x80FF8000 to reset the chip, waits for busy to clear and returns the original error.

items.title: NAND chip identification
items.text:
After reset succeeds, init_nand (0x20000318, process 2 virtual address) sends Read ID (0x90) with column address zero and reads 64 bytes into nand_chip_id (0x200091C0). It compares the first two bytes with the manufacturer and device bytes of each entry in nand_chip_table (0x20008000). The table holds ten 68 byte entries.

The accepted manufacturer/device pairs are AD 76, AD F1, AD DC, EC 76, EC F1, EC DA, EC DC, 98 76, 98 F1 and 98 DA. If no entry matches, initialization releases its event and queues, disables the NAND interface and returns -9.

items.title: SEEPROM
items.text: SEEPROM is a serial EEPROM accessed through GPIO. boot1 uses it for version records and IOS reads it for console certificate data.

items.title: GPIO connection
items.text:
Address Width Access Name Purpose 0x0D8000E0 32 bits R/W HW_GPIO1OUT Chip select, clock and outgoing data 0x0D8000E8 32 bits R HW_GPIO1IN Incoming data Register Bits Name Description HW_GPIO1OUT 10 Chip select High during a transfer HW_GPIO1OUT 11 Clock Serial clock HW_GPIO1OUT 12 Data out Data sent to SEEPROM HW_GPIO1IN 13 Data in Data received from SEEPROM

For each outgoing bit, they lower the clock, assert chip select and set the data output before raising the clock. For each incoming bit, they lower the clock, assert chip select and raise the clock before sampling the input. They end a transfer by clearing chip select and issuing two clock pulses, leaving the clock low.

items.title: Firmware commands
items.text:
Operation Command Following transfer Read word 11 bits: 0x600 OR word_address Receive 16 bits Write word 11 bits: 0x500 OR word_address Send 16 bits Enable writes 11 bits: 0x4C0 None Disable writes 11 bits: 0x400 None

IOS enables writes before writing a record and disables them afterwards. After each word write, it ends the transfer then polls the input in groups of 10 bits. The last bit of each group indicates readiness. It ends the polling transfer when that bit is 1 or the retry limit is reached.

items.title: Certificate data
items.text:
IOS reads the following fields for the console certificate. Offsets are byte offsets within SEEPROM. Integer fields are big-endian.

Offset Size Contents 0x00 4 bytes MS identifier 0x04 4 bytes CA identifier 0x08 4 bytes NG key identifier 0x0C 60 bytes NG certificate signature

The MS and CA identifiers form the certificate issuer components. The NG device identifier comes from OTP, separately from the NG key identifier stored here. See IOS certificate identity.

boot1's version records begin at byte offset 0x48.

items.title: IOS
items.text:
IOS is the operating system that runs on Starlet. It provides the filesystem, ES (eTicket Services) and device drivers. boot2 loads IOS from the NAND filesystem. The loaded IOS starts its own kernel and modules, including the DI (Disc Interface) and OHCI (USB Open Host Controller Interface) drivers.

IOS58 also includes an EHCI (USB 2.0) driver.

items.title: IOS80 modules
items.text:
IOS80 v6944 contains the following module tags in its embedded IOSVersion strings:

Content ID Tag 0x00000001 DIP 0x00000002 OH0 0x00000003 OH1 0x00000004 SDI 0x00000005 SO 0x00000006 KD 0x00000007 WD 0x00000010 WL 0x00000009 NCD 0x0000000A ETH 0x0000000B STM 0x0000000C KBD 0x0000000D SSL 0x0000000E IOSP, FSP and ES

items.title: System Menu launch
items.text:
boot2 selects the System Menu title 00000001-00000002 and loads its required IOS. It carries the launch request across the IOS reload in /sys/launch.sys. The file starts with an 8 byte big-endian title ID followed by a 0xD8 byte ticket view.

During startup, es_worker (0x201015E8) reads this file, obtains the title metadata and configures IPC access rights before calling launch_title (0x20104CF4). The title's boot content is passed to load_executable (0xFFFF0E8C). For a DOL, the loader clears BSS and loads the text and data sections into RAM.

prepare_broadway (0xFFFF0E40) installs the 64 byte g_broadway_reset_stub (0xFFFF8880) through EXI. The stub sets SRR0 to 0x00003400, clears SRR1 and executes rfi. The loaded executable supplies the code at 0x00003400.

Address Width Register IOS use 0x0D800034 32 bits HW_PPCIRQMASK Enables the Broadway IPC interrupt. 0x0D800070 32 bits HW_EXICTRL Controls EXI access around boot-code setup. 0x0D800180 32 bits HW_DIFLAGS Selects the uploaded boot code. 0x0D800194 32 bits HW_RESETS Sequences Broadway reset. 0x0D806840 through 0x0D80687F 32 bit writes EXI boot-code window Holds 16 instruction words. Register Bits Firmware operation HW_PPCIRQMASK 30 Set before releasing Broadway. HW_EXICTRL 0 Set while uploading the stub, cleared before reset release and set again afterwards. HW_DIFLAGS 20 Set after uploading the stub. HW_RESETS 5:4 Both cleared first, then bit 5 is set and finally bit 4 is set.

reset_broadway (0xFFFF678C) performs the reset sequence after loading the executable. The uploaded stub runs from Broadway's reset vector at 0xFFF00100 and transfers execution to the loaded title.
